theme: The twelve spies; the faithless report; forty years
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 13:1-14:45. This is the turning point of the book and one of the saddest chapters in the Old Testament. Read it as the story of a failure of faith, and note carefully what the people say, and what God says in reply.
settingTheScene: Israel has come to the edge of Canaan, at Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran. God tells Moses to send twelve men, one from each tribe, to explore the land. They go for forty days and return with a report. Ten say the land is good but its people are too strong. Two, Joshua and Caleb, say that God will give it to them. The people believe the ten. What follows is the decisive failure of the exodus generation.
observation: God says, “Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel” (13:2).
The spies bring back a cluster of grapes so large that it is carried on a pole by two men (13:23).
All twelve agree: “It flows with milk and honey” (13:27).
Ten report: “We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we… we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers” (13:31-33).
Caleb says, “Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it” (13:30).
The people weep and say, “Would that we had died in the land of Egypt!” and propose to choose a leader and go back (14:1-4).
Moses pleads for the people, appealing to God’s name: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (14:13-19).
God pardons them, but says that none of the men who saw his signs and yet tested him ten times shall see the land. Their children will enter, after forty years of wandering (14:20-35).
interpretation:
The sin here is not caution. It is unbelief. God had already said that he was giving them the land. The spies were not sent to decide whether to go, but to see what God was giving. When ten of them look at the land and then look at themselves, they forget God. Their report shifts from “the land flows with milk and honey” to “the land devours its inhabitants.” And their self-image shrinks: “we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers.” Fear distorts how we see ourselves and how we see God.

Joshua and Caleb saw the same land and the same giants. The difference was not in what they saw, but in what they believed about God. Caleb says, “we are well able,” and Joshua says, “the LORD is with us; do not fear them.” Faith does not deny the giants. It remembers who is bigger.

The people’s reaction is a tragedy. They weep all night. They say they wish they had died in Egypt, and they even say that God brought them out because he hates them (Deuteronomy 1:27). They call good evil. In a few hours, they undo the whole exodus in their minds.

Moses’ intercession is a high point. He does not argue that Israel deserves mercy. He argues from God’s own character, quoting the words of Exodus 34:6-7. And God does pardon the people, but he does not remove the consequences. The generation that refused to enter will not enter. Forgiveness and discipline are both real.

The last scene shows how unbelief hardens into presumption. When told they will not enter, the people suddenly decide to attack on their own. Without God, they are defeated. Obedience delayed is not the same as obedience. They had refused to go when God said go, and now they went when God said no.
connection: Hebrews 3 and 4 use this story as a warning to the church. “Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God” (Hebrews 3:12). The generation “were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). The promise of rest still stands, and Jesus, whose name is the same as Joshua’s, leads us in. Paul says that these events were written down for our instruction (1 Corinthians 10:11).
application:
Ask what giant you are facing, and whether you are seeing it through your own eyes or God’s promise.

Is there something God has told you to do that you are delaying? Obey today, not later.

Pray for the courage of Joshua and Caleb, to speak the truth even when the crowd is afraid.
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you have been looking at giants instead of promises.
Confess your unbelief and ask for a spirit like Caleb’s.
Thank Jesus for leading his people into rest.
